Why is Disney eating the scraps of bankrupt Character.AI?

Fact check on these words (1 November 2026): every other line passed or was already signed off by Krish. 3 lines need his sign-off in his own words before publishing: "Google hired Character.AI's founders in August 2024, two years before the bankruptcy; OpenAI said it would shut its Sora video app; and the court filing warned about cash and litigation." | "The founders leaving was the first warning sign in this story, and it was easy to miss." | "That's our inference from the timing and the filings; Disney hasn't said it in those words."Prediction kept as recorded (1 March 2027, 75%)Both cuts watched in full and approved by Krish on 28 October 2026

The idea, the story's flow, the ending, the takeaway, the angle and the tone, agreed before the drafts are written.

Record-ready briefAgreed 26 Oct
The idea
Why did Google and Disney both pay for Character.AI, and what does it mean for any business that runs on someone else's AI?
The story, beat by beat
  1. Google paid for the brains: a reported $2.7 billion in 2024 for the tech, and it hired the founders.
  2. Disney tried renting first: a $1 billion deal to put 200+ characters in OpenAI's Sora, which OpenAI shut in March.
  3. Now Disney is buying the team: 66 staff at about $60 million a year, and a $20 million opening bid for the code, through a bankruptcy it required.
  4. Who is left with the shell: the users and the lawsuits stay with Character.AI.
  5. Our prediction: by 1 March 2027, Skydance, Universal Music Group and Comcast's NBCUniversal each announce buying an AI company or its team (75%).
The ending
Here's what I'd do with this info if I were you: ask four things about the firm behind your main AI tool. Founders still there? Main product or side bet? Short of cash? Collecting lawsuits?
The takeaway
The money followed the people, and everyone else was left with the empty box. Watch your AI supplier for the warning signs years before the end.
The angle
follow.the.money: two giants, two receipts, one empty box.
The tone
Observational and witty, dry on true details (Disney 'respected the decision').
Who it is for
A leader whose business leans on AI tools made by someone else.

The article and the scripts. Edit any paragraph or comment on any passage; your saves and comments shape the next version.

The words are signed off. The article is under Publish, in its first step; the scripts are under Record.

Video script (5-minute cut)
Disney asked a dying AI firm to go bust first. That way it could hire the team and leave the lawsuits behind. So why are Disney and Google both paying for pieces of the same company? And what does it mean for you?

I've been reading the court papers on Character.AI, the app where millions of people chat with made-up characters. Two giants have now paid for pieces of it, for very different reasons. So I wanted to break it down for you.

Let's start with Google. Google wanted the brains behind the app. So in 2024, it reportedly paid two point seven billion dollars to use Character.AI's tech. And it hired the founders and their research team away. Google was racing to build the smartest AI, and these people were very good at it. But the rest of the staff stayed behind, and the app carried on, until its cash started running low.

Now, Disney wanted something else, and to see why, go back to last December. Disney agreed to put a billion dollars into OpenAI. As part of that deal, over two hundred Disney characters would star in Sora, OpenAI's video app. But Sora belonged to OpenAI. So Disney was really renting space for Mickey, Marvel and Star Wars on someone else's app.

Then in March, OpenAI shut Sora down. The deal died, and no money changed hands. Disney said it respected the decision, which is a very polite way to say, well, that's awkward.

So Disney changed its plan. In September, it hired Character.AI's chief executive, who ran the firm after the founders left. He got a brand new job, Disney's first ever technology chief. And this month, the court papers show the rest of the plan. Disney has offered jobs to sixty-six of Character.AI's staff. All together, their pay comes to about sixty million dollars a year, for three years. On top of that, Disney has bid twenty million dollars for the code. That includes its tools for keeping children safe.

Here's the clever bit. Character.AI filed for bankruptcy on the twelfth of October. And Disney made that a condition of its offer, and the papers even say why. Character.AI was running low on cash. And it faced lawsuits from families and US states, who say its chatbots harmed children. Going through the court means Disney takes the people and the code, clean, while the lawsuits stay behind with Character.AI.

So who is left holding the empty box? The people who used the app, for a start. Disney didn't bid for the app itself, or for anyone's chats. So what happens to the app is now up to the court. And then there are the people suing Character.AI, whose claims stay with a firm that is being sold for parts.

See, the money followed the people. Google paid billions for the tech and the founders, and Disney is paying millions for the rest of the team. Everyone else is left with the empty box.

And it isn't just Disney. Netflix bought an AI film start-up this year, and the record label Warner Music bought an AI firm too. The big media firms have stopped renting AI, and started owning it.

So my prediction is that three more giants follow them. First, Skydance, the new owner of Paramount Pictures. Then the record label Universal Music. And then Comcast, the American TV giant that owns NBC. By the first of March, 2027, I reckon each of them will announce buying an AI firm or its team. And I'm seventy-five percent sure all three will do it.

Now, why should you care if you're not Disney? Because most businesses now run on someone else's AI. It might be your writing tool, your chatbot, or maybe your whole customer service desk. If that supplier goes the way of Sora, the tool can switch off. And your work in it can go too. And this story shows the warning signs, years before the end.

Here's what I'd do with this info if I were you. Pick the AI tool your business leans on most, and ask four things about the firm that makes it. First, are its founders still there? Google took Character.AI's founders two years before the end. Second, is your tool the main thing that firm sells, or a side bet? Sora was a side bet, and it vanished. Third, is the firm running short of cash? The court papers warned about exactly that. And fourth, is it collecting lawsuits? That's why Disney went through the court. If two of those answers worry you, line up a plan B now. That means a second tool you've tried on real work, and a copy of your own data.

The full deep dive is at makeyourmindup.ai.
Video script (90-second cut)
I've been reading court papers on Character.AI, a chat app with millions of users. It ran low on cash, faced lawsuits over harm to children, and went bust. So why did Google, and now Disney, both pay for it?

Google got the brains first. In 2024 it reportedly paid two point seven billion dollars to use the tech, and hired the founders away.

Disney wanted its characters in AI videos, so it agreed a billion-dollar deal with OpenAI's video app, Sora. Then OpenAI shut Sora down.

So Disney is building its own team, hiring sixty-six staff on sixty million dollars a year in total. And by buying through the bankruptcy court, Disney leaves the lawsuits behind.

So my prediction? I reckon that by March 2027, Skydance, Universal Music and Comcast each buy an AI team too. I'm seventy-five percent sure all three will.

Here's what I'd do with this info if I were you. Ask four things about the firm behind your AI. Are its founders still there? Is your tool its main product? Is it short of cash? And is it piling up lawsuits?

Title
Why is Disney eating the scraps of bankrupt Character.AI?
Subtitle
Why did Google and Disney both pay for Character.AI, and what does it mean for any business that runs on someone else's AI?
The article, with its pictures in place

Disney would only take on a dying AI company's team through the bankruptcy court, so it could hire the team and leave the lawsuits behind.

That company is Character.AI, the app where millions of people chat with made-up characters. It filed for bankruptcy in Delaware on 12 October. Google and Disney have now paid for pieces of it, two years apart, for two very different reasons. And the people who used it are left holding whatever remains.

This piece follows why Google and Disney both paid for Character.AI, and what that means for any business that runs on someone else's AI.

GOOGLE PAID FOR THE BRAINS

In August 2024, Google reportedly paid $2.7 billion to license Character.AI's technology. A spokesperson told Wired that the licence covered the technology as it stood at the time, and that Google also hired the founders and other members of their research team.

The "vast majority" of the staff stayed at Character.AI, the same spokesperson said. The app kept running too, as if nothing much had happened.

Our read on Google is simple: it wanted the people who built Character.AI, and a licence to use what they had built. So it paid for both, and left the company standing.

Keep that date in your head. August 2024 is when the founders went to Google. The bankruptcy came in October 2026. The founders leaving was the first warning sign in this story, and it was easy to miss.

DISNEY TRIED RENTING FIRST

Disney's reason starts somewhere else entirely.

In December 2025, Disney agreed to put $1 billion into OpenAI and to let more than 200 of its characters appear in Sora, OpenAI's video app. Marvel, Pixar and Star Wars would all be in there. A big bet, with one catch: every one of those characters would live on someone else's app.

Then in March 2026, OpenAI said it would shut its Sora app. The Disney deal went with it, and reports say no money had changed hands. Disney said it respected the decision, which is the corporate way of saying it had just been left standing in the rain.

We think the rest of the story turns on this moment. Disney had licensed its characters to someone else's app, and that app closed.

NOW DISNEY IS BUYING THE TEAM

So Disney changed its approach. In September it hired Character.AI's chief executive as its first chief technology officer.

As for why Disney chose Character.AI out of every AI company it could have picked, look at what each side owns. Disney owns Marvel, Pixar and Star Wars, and Character.AI's app lets millions of people chat with made-up characters. After Sora, Disney seems to have decided it would rather own the team that does this than rent space on someone else's app. That's our inference from the timing and the filings; Disney hasn't said it in those words.

Then came the court papers. Disney has offered jobs to 66 of Character.AI's staff, most of the workforce. Their pay comes to about $60 million a year for three years, around $180 million in all, according to the filings reported by Gizmodo. On top of that, Disney has made the opening $20 million bid for rights to Character.AI's technology, a bid other buyers can still beat. Wired reports that the list of what Disney is bidding for covers its code, its trust and safety tools, its training infrastructure and its age-prediction technology.

Here's the part we keep coming back to. The filings say Disney required the deal to go through the bankruptcy court, because of Character.AI's "diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks". Wired reports that a draft court order would leave Character.AI responsible for "any liability or other obligation" it might have.

If the court approves, Disney gets the people and much of the code. Character.AI keeps the legal fights.

WHO IS LEFT WITH THE SHELL

Two groups stay behind.

First, the people who used the app. According to Wired, the list of what Disney is bidding for leaves out users' data and Character.AI's website, and the court filing leaves out its consumer-facing apps. What happens to the app now is up to the court. Anyone who spent two years chatting to a made-up character on there will want to know where those chats end up.

Second, everyone with a claim against it. Families sued Character.AI, saying its chatbots harmed children; those families agreed to settle, and a referee approved each settlement on 11 October, the day before the bankruptcy. When it filed, 46 states and territories were investigating it, and several states have sued. Wired reports the deal is built so that whatever is left of Character.AI keeps responsibility for those legal battles, some of them still going.

So the money followed the people. Google reportedly paid $2.7 billion to use the tech and hire the founders. Disney is offering about $180 million in pay to most of the rest of the staff, plus a $20 million bid for the technology. Everyone else gets the empty box.

If your business runs on someone else's AI, this is the part worth sitting with. You can't stop your supplier being bought or shut down. You can spot the signs early, and in this story they showed up years before the end.

OUR PREDICTION

Beyond Disney, our read is that the companies with the most to lose are deciding that renting their AI is too risky.

Disney isn't alone. This year Netflix bought InterPositive, an AI filmmaking start-up, in a deal reported at $587 million. Warner Music bought Sureel AI in June. WildBrain, the company behind the Teletubbies, bought Personality AI in August.

Put those together and a pattern shows. The big media companies are moving from renting AI to owning it.

Three of the biggest haven't made that move yet. Skydance, which now owns Paramount and Warner Bros after its merger closed on 6 October, calls the combined company "tech-forward". Universal Music has struck agreements with AI companies, including Nvidia, but we could find none it has bought, while its rival Warner Music has. NBCUniversal has made no AI purchase that we could find.

Each of them now has a rival that has bought, and Disney has just shown everyone what renting can cost. That's why we think they move next.

Our prediction. By 1 March 2027, Skydance, Universal Music Group and Comcast's NBCUniversal will each have announced buying an AI company or its team. How sure we are: 75%.

It isn't higher because all three have to move inside about four months, and any one of them could decide that renting is fine for now.

If the giants with the deepest pockets won't leave their AI in someone else's hands, it's worth knowing whose hands yours is in.

3 things you can do tomorrow

  1. Write down the AI tools your business would struggle without, and who makes each one. Most leaders know the tools. Fewer know whether the maker is a giant, a start-up or a giant's side project.
  2. For the one you lean on most, answer four questions about its maker. Are its founders still there? Is your tool its main product or a side bet? Is it short of cash? Is it collecting lawsuits? Google hired Character.AI's founders in August 2024, two years before the bankruptcy; OpenAI said it would shut its Sora video app; and the court filing warned about cash and litigation.
  3. If two of those answers worry you, pick your plan B now. Choose the tool you would move to, and try it on one real task this month, while you still have time to switch calmly.

5-minute script

749 words

You've probably danced to this song. It's called Movin' To The Sun, and this autumn it got to number two in the UK charts. And here's the twist: it started on an AI app. So is it AI music or human music?

And it isn't the only one. There's another song called Bad Times that started the same way. And the woman who wrote them both had never made music in her life.

I've been digging into how these songs were made, and it's a cracking story. So who really made them? I want to break it down for you. There are three parts: who wrote it, who finished it, and what the Grammys made of it.

Part one, who wrote it. The writer goes by the name Imael Angel. She's a Reiki master, which is a kind of healer who works with their hands. She's written children's books. What she had never done is write a song.

So she typed her words into an AI music app. You give it some lyrics and a style, and it makes you a whole song in minutes. The tune, the backing and even the singing voice all come out of the app. So the first version of the song was sung by a voice that belongs to no one.

And then she put the songs out online. People used them as the background music on their short videos, under clips of cats and family weddings. Viewers heard a song behind someone else's clip and wanted to know what it was. Loads of the comments online are just people asking, what's this song?

So AI got her in the door. Not long ago, a healer with no studio and no band would have had no way in. Now she had songs that strangers were hunting for.

Part two, who finished it. This is where the humans come in. A dance producer called HUGEL heard Movin' To The Sun and rebuilt it by hand. He played the parts again himself, and he brought in Ultra Naté to sing it. She's a real singer with real hits behind her. That version went to number two and stayed in the charts for months.

The second song went the same way. A human singer sang it again and human producers rebuilt it. Then one of the biggest record companies in the world put it out.

So ask yourself this. Is it an AI song? The idea was hers, but the first voice was a machine. Then a human rebuilt the track, and the voice you hear now is human too. And there's still a thin layer of the AI voice tucked in underneath Ultra Naté's.

Part three, what the Grammys made of it. The Grammys are the biggest awards in music. They give one prize for writing a song, and another for singing it. So they had to decide which prizes this song could even go up for. And they gave it two answers at once. The writing prize covers the music as well as the words. And the song still uses parts that the app made. So it can't go up for the writing. But it can go up for the singing, because a human sang it.

So one song is AI and human at the same time. Even the people whose whole job is judging music couldn't make it one thing or the other.

And the people dancing to it? Most of them don't seem to care. Under the singer's own video, hardly anyone even mentions AI. The top comments are people saying it makes them feel young again.

So here's the one thing to remember. I reckon AI against human is the wrong fight. AI got someone new in the door, and people carried the song the rest of the way. A person's idea, an AI voice, a human rebuild and a human singer: it's both, all the way through.

And that's happening in every kind of work now. Adverts, reports, even the work your own team hands you. So asking whether it's AI or human tells you less and less. But asking who did which bit tells you what to check, and who to thank.

So the next time someone hands me a song, an advert or a report, I'll ask one thing. Who did which bit? Because the song you can't stop dancing to is already both, and that's how music gets made now.

The full deep dive is at makeyourmindup.ai.

  1. Cold open: Hanoi, 1902, a cent a rat tail, so people farmed rats.
  2. The mandates: Shopify, Duolingo, Microsoft and Coinbase judge staff on AI use.

Article

1,402 words

In 1902, the French rulers of Hanoi had a rat problem, so they paid a bounty of one cent for every rat tail handed in. The tails poured in. Then people started seeing rats in the streets with no tails, very much alive. Hunters were snipping off the tails and letting the rats go, so they could breed and grow more tails. Some set up rat farms on the edge of the city.

Hanoi wanted dead rats, and it paid for tails, so tails are what it got.

Over the past 18 months, some of the biggest companies in the world ran that experiment again with AI. They told their staff to use it, counted how much they used it, ranked them on it and then backed off without much fuss. This piece is about why counting how much AI your people use makes things worse, and what to count instead.

A CENT A RAT TAIL

Historian Michael Vann pieced the Hanoi story together from the colonial archives, in a 2003 paper for the journal French Colonial History. Hanoi had just built modern sewers, and they turned out to be a superb home for rats (nobody had asked the rats). Plague was the fear. Paid hunters went down into the tunnels, and when that wasn't enough, the city opened the bounty to everyone.

A tail was the proof because it was small, easy to carry and easy to count. A whole dead rat was none of those things. And that's the trap. Whatever you can count is rarely what you actually want, and once money rides on the count, people get very good at producing it. Hanoi learned that with rats. In 2025, big companies started learning it with AI.

THE MANDATES

It began sensibly enough. In April 2025, Shopify's chief executive, Tobi Lütke, sent his staff a memo that he then posted in public. "Reflexive AI usage is now a baseline expectation at Shopify," it said, and it added questions about AI use to performance reviews.

That same month, Duolingo's chief executive, Luis von Ahn, told staff the company would look at AI use when it judged performance. At Coinbase, chief executive Brian Armstrong later said he had fired engineers who would not start using the company's AI coding tools.

Each of these leaders had a fair point. AI tools only help if people actually pick them up, and plenty of staff were ignoring them. But the moment AI use went into a performance review, it turned into a score. And people know what to do with a score.

THE LEADERBOARDS

Once something is a score, someone builds a chart of it.

At Meta, the owner of Facebook, one employee built an internal leaderboard nicknamed "Claudeonomics". Fortune reported in April 2026 that it ranked around 85,000 staff by how many tokens they had used. Tokens are the small chunks of words an AI reads and writes, and every one of them costs money. It handed out titles such as "Token Legend" and "Cache Wizard" (somebody had fun naming those), and staff got through 60 trillion tokens in 30 days. It came down about two days after the story broke.

Amazon had its own version. Kiro is Amazon's AI coding tool, and an unofficial board called KiroRank ranked staff by how much they used it. CIO reported in May 2026 that some staff set AI agents, programs that keep working on a task by themselves, running on unnecessary tasks just to push up their scores.

One engineer's post caught the mood: "Whenever my PM says something ridiculous I launch 10 sub-agents to analyse him." It was a joke. But the leaderboards meant the joke paid.

That's the rat tail again. Each board counted AI use, and AI use is what it got: lots of it, and no way to tell how much of it did anything.

THE U-TURNS

Then the companies running the boards turned round.

KiroRank was taken offline, and a senior Amazon vice president said the computing costs of all that usage were too high. In September 2026, Meta said it would no longer use AI adoption dashboards or token counts to judge performance.

Amazon made the clearest statement in October. CNBC reported new guidance telling its engineers that token counts and similar usage numbers are "deeply flawed" measures of success. That guidance also says that when an engineer tries AI on a job and it doesn't help, that is "a finding, not a failing".

That last line matters more than it looks. Once failing to use AI counts against you, nobody admits the AI didn't help. They just keep it running. Usage goes up, and the information you actually needed, where AI works and where it doesn't, disappears.

HALF THE TARGET, MORE SALES

A study posted to arXiv this autumn shows what happens when a company counts less, and its answer is unusually clean.

Its authors looked at one large medical-device company with about 5,000 staff. It had set a target of 200 AI queries a month per person. When the researchers looked at what people were actually asking, 31% of the queries were repeats or had nothing to do with work. People were hitting their number.

So the company cut the target in half, to 100. Total AI use fell by about 30%, and about 90% of that drop was the junk. The real use stayed. And monthly sales went up 7%.

It rolled the change out branch by branch, so the researchers could compare branches that had the lower target with branches that didn't yet. That's what lets them say the cut did it, rather than a good month.

Read that again from a manager's seat. It asked for less AI and got more of what it was actually paying for. Those junk queries had cost money and time, and they had buried the useful work in noise.

THE COBRA THAT NEVER WAS

There's a twist. Ask anyone for the famous story about counting the wrong thing, and you'll get cobras. Under British rule in Delhi, so it goes, the government paid for dead cobras, so people bred cobras for the bounty, and when the bounty ended they let them go, leaving the city with more snakes than before.

It's a great story. It is also very hard to prove. The Juggernaut, which went looking, found little evidence to support it. "Cobra effect", the phrase, was coined in 2001 by the German economist Horst Siebert, and the tale has been repeated ever since, mostly by people warning others to check their numbers.

So even the warning got believed without anyone checking it. Hanoi's rat tails, meanwhile, are in the archives.

Both stories point the same way. A count feels like proof, so we stop asking what's behind it. That's as true of an AI usage dashboard as it is of a bag of tails.

For the business, this is the practical bit. A usage number tells you people did more of the thing you counted, and nothing else. What matters is what got done: more sales, faster answers to customers, fewer hours on the monthly report. If a team's AI use doubles and none of those moves, you've bought a lot of rat tails.

Our prediction. By 30 June 2027, Shopify will say in public that it no longer uses AI usage as a measure in its performance reviews. Meta and Amazon have already backed away, and a company that put usage questions into its reviews in April 2025 is unlikely to keep them once its peers call the measure flawed. How sure we are: 65%.

It isn't higher because Shopify can change its reviews without saying so, and a change nobody announces is a change we can't check.

3 things you can do tomorrow

  1. Scrap any target or ranking for how much AI people use. If a dashboard, a review form or a team goal counts prompts, tokens or logins, take that line out.
  2. Make "AI didn't help here" a good answer. Amazon now calls it "a finding, not a failing". Say the same to your team, so nobody fakes their usage to look keen.
  3. Judge AI on a number you already track. Pick one, such as sales, tickets closed or invoices sent. If it hasn't moved, the AI isn't working yet, whatever the usage says.

5-minute script

806 words

In 1902, the city of Hanoi had a rat problem. So it paid people for every rat tail they handed in, as proof of a dead rat. What could possibly go wrong?

And people did hand in tails, lots of them. But then rats with no tails started turning up in the streets, very much alive. People were snipping off the tails and letting the rats go, to breed more tails. Some even set up rat farms.

Now, that's a funny old story. Hanoi paid for tails, when what it wanted was dead rats. And big companies just made the same mistake with AI. It took them less than two years to try it, regret it and undo it.

I've been digging into how companies measure AI at work, and it matters to anyone who runs a team. So why does counting how much AI your people use make things worse? I want to break it down for you. There are three parts: the rules, the leaderboards and the U-turns.

Part one, the rules. In 2025, bosses started telling staff that using AI wasn't optional. Shopify's boss told his people to reach for AI first, as a habit. Duolingo said it would look at AI use in performance reviews. And lots of other firms did the same. So using AI became something you got marked on at work.

Part two, the leaderboards. And once you're marking something, someone builds a chart. Take Meta, the owner of Facebook. One of its staff built a board that ranked people by how much AI they used. AI use is counted in tokens, which are small chunks of words the AI reads and writes. And every one of them costs money. So the more you asked the AI to do, the higher you climbed.

And the board gave out titles. The top users were called things like Token Legend. Amazon has an AI coding tool called Kiro, and it had its own version, called KiroRank.

You can guess what happened next. People wanted to climb. Now, there are bits of AI called agents, which keep working on a task by themselves. So some people set agents running on pointless jobs, just to burn more tokens. One engineer even joked online about it. Whenever a colleague said something silly, the engineer set a whole gang of agents off to pick it apart. That helps no one, but it does climb the board. It was a joke. But the leaderboard was real.

So the rat tails were back. There was loads of AI use, and not much to show for it.

Part three, the U-turns. Meta's board came down within days of the press reporting on it. Then Meta said it would no longer use AI counts to judge people in their reviews. Amazon shut KiroRank down too, and one of its bosses said the AI bills were just too high. And this autumn Amazon told its engineers that counting AI use was deeply flawed.

Here's the bit I like most. Researchers looked at a big firm that makes medical equipment. It gave its staff a monthly target for AI use. About a third of that use turned out to be junk. People asked the same thing twice, or asked about things that had nothing to do with work. They were just hitting their number. So the firm cut the target in half. The junk dropped away, the real use stayed, and sales went up by 7%. And the researchers compared branches with the cut to branches without it, so they could see the cut did it.

So they asked for less AI, and they sold more.

Now, there's a twist. The most famous story about this mistake is about cobras in India. The British paid for dead cobras, so people bred cobras. Everyone tells it. But historians can't find good proof that it ever happened. So even the warning about counting the wrong thing got believed without anyone checking it. The rats in Hanoi, though, are in the records.

And I reckon that's the real lesson of both stories, from the rats to AI. A number feels like proof, so we stop checking what's behind it. But a count only tells you people did more of the thing you counted.

So here's the one thing to remember. Whatever you count, people learn to make more of it. Count AI use, and you get AI use. Count the work that got done, and you get work.

If you're counting how much AI your people use, you're counting rat tails.

If I ran a team, I'd do one thing this week. I'd delete any target for AI use. And I'd check if the AI is moving a number I already track, like sales or invoices sent.

The full deep dive is at makeyourmindup.ai.
